items.title: Slide Hampton — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: The interviewee discusses Tadd Dameron's music and influence in the context of jazz history and repertory, stating 'the music of Monk and Tadd Dameron and Dizzy, they developed all that music together' and 'They should be playing Tadd Dameron.' There is no mention of a personal meeting, collaboratio

ctx.x: How much – do you believe it would be possible to focus on Tadd’s music and Dizzy’s music? How much more music is there in . . . ? People will say things like, people haven’t caught up to Bird yet. People haven’t figured out, haven’t really fully explored Dizzy yet. Does that mean, in your mind, that there’s, within that body of composition – I’ll throw Tadd and there and some others, with Dizzy, Bird things, things that Monk did – that there’s a whole world of music there yet to be explored?

Yes, there is, because the music of Monk and Tadd Dameron and Dizzy, they developed all that music together. The influence that they each had on each other is what inspired them to compose the music that they composed. When the people think of Dizzy, they should also think of Monk, because Monk and Dizzy did a lot of that developing together. A lot of the things that Monk composed inspired Dizzy to do what he did, and vice versa, and Tadd Dameron, and several guys. It was a whole group of people that were working…
You think there are a lot of musical ideas there that are still to be mined.

items.title: Slide Hampton — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: No, we only performed with Tadd’s material.

ctx.x: Did that group perform other material?
No, we only performed with Tadd’s material.
